posts.hook: Meta just published how agencies are testing incrementality. Incrementality means asking: did the ad cause the sale, or would that person have bought anyway?
posts.body:
Meta just published how agencies are testing incrementality.

Incrementality means asking: did the ad cause the sale, or would that person have bought anyway?

Most small advertisers never check this. They look at "results" in Ads Manager and assume every one came from the ad. Meta's own post admits that is not always true, and shows agencies running holdout tests to find out — showing the ad to one group and not another, then comparing what each group actually bought.

You don't need an agency's budget to borrow the idea. Pick your best-spending campaign. Pause it for a few days in a market or audience segment you can isolate, and watch if sales actually drop, or barely move.

If sales barely move, that budget wasn't creating buyers. It was catching people who were going to buy anyway, and the ad got the credit.

This is the same discipline behind every number I publish — cost per lead means amount spent divided by leads counted in Meta's own lead centre, nothing modelled. Incrementality testing is that same honesty, aimed at the sale itself.

Have you ever turned a campaign off on purpose, just to see what happens to sales without it?

Nine Meta ad accounts. One order, every time, before touching a single ad.

Most people fixing a slow account start with the creative — new image, new headline, new offer. That's usually step six, not step one.

Before any of that, there's a fixed order: check what the campaign is actually optimised to do, check what the ad set calls success, check where the lead actually lands, check who looks at it and when. Only after all of that is cleared does the creative get touched.

Across 7,341 lead-form submissions on nine accounts, the leak was almost never the ad itself. It was somewhere upstream or downstream of it — a setting nobody opened in months, or a lead nobody followed up within the hour.

The order matters because fixing creative on a broken foundation just gets you a prettier version of the same leak.

slides.text: Nobody checks this before touching the creative.
Changing the ad first just makes the real leak harder to find.
Start in Ads Manager, not the ad. Open your campaign and find the Performance goal line first.

Fix the account in this order: goal, ad set, form, follow-up. Creative comes last, not first.

Google just published a holiday shopping guide built on search data, not guesses.

Most small businesses read that as "big brand news" and move on. The distinction that matters: it's not about ad budgets, it's about timing — when people start searching before they buy.

Here's the mechanic worth knowing. Google tracks search interest by category and publishes when it peaks, weeks before the actual buying date. If you sell anything seasonal, that peak is when your ad or your Google Business Profile needs to already be live, not when you finally get around to it.

Most small accounts do the opposite. They start campaigns the week they feel ready, not the week their customer starts looking. By the time the ad goes live, the searcher has already bought from whoever showed up first.

This costs nothing to check. Go to Google Trends, type your product category, and look at the last two years. The search spike repeats on roughly the same week every year.

What week does your category's search interest actually spike, and is your account live before it or during it?

Cost per lead means nothing if the campaign funding your best leads is the one getting starved first. Check which campaign is marked top priority before you check anything else this week.

If your reach drops next month, the first question is not "did the algorithm hate me" — it's whether the audience told it to want less of what you're posting.

I'm doing a few free audits of ad accounts this month for anyone who wants a second pair of eyes on this.

posts.hook: One line in a lead form decides whether your sales team talks to buyers, or to browsers. Most forms ask for name, phone, email. That tells you nothing about whether the person can actually buy what you sell.
posts.body:
One line in a lead form decides whether your sales team talks to buyers, or to browsers.

Most forms ask for name, phone, email. That tells you nothing about whether the person can actually buy what you sell.

A Tirupur apparel manufacturer ran a campaign where the ad and the form both stated a 200-piece minimum order, up front. 19 wholesale buyers responded, at under $6 an enquiry.

Compare that to the same manufacturer's wider lead campaigns: 4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each across six campaigns. Cheaper leads, no qualifying question in front of them.

Neither number is wrong. They are two different products. Cheap leads fill a sheet. Qualified leads fill a sales call.

The qualifying question is not about your product. It is about the one thing that would make someone unable to buy from you at all — minimum order size, budget, location, timeline. Put that one thing in the form, in plain words, before you ask for a phone number.

You will get fewer leads. You will also stop handing your sales team people who were never going to say yes.

The point is simpler: a generation is about to grow up treating AI as the default way to ask a question, not a novelty. That changes what a search, a form fill or an enquiry even looks like in a few years.

If you run ads today, nothing in your account needs to change tomorrow because of this. But the people filling your lead forms five years from now learned to ask AI before they learned to Google. Nobody can tell you exactly what that means for cost per lead yet. Anyone who says they can is guessing. What you can do today is keep your own numbers honest, so when the shift shows up in your account, you notice it in your data and not in a feeling.

GPT-6 landed this week. "Intelligent UI" builds the screen for your question, not the other way round.

Most posts will stop at that headline. Here's what it means if you run your own ads.

An interface that writes itself still needs you to know what you're asking for. Ask ChatGPT to "check my Meta campaign" and it can read a screenshot. It cannot open Ads Manager, click into your ad set, and tell you your Performance goal is set to Conversations when you meant Purchases.

That gap is where cost per lead actually gets decided. Not in the chat window — inside the account, in a setting most people never open.

Smarter tools change what you can ask. They don't change what you need to know to ask it well. A founder who can't read a lifetime view in Ads Manager will get a very fluent wrong answer, faster than before.

Across nine of our own ad accounts, every lead is still counted the same way it always was: a submission in Meta's lead centre, tied to the ad and form that produced it. No model, no estimate.

If you want a second set of eyes on how your account is actually set up, before you hand the thinking to a chatbot, that's something we do for free on jothiswaroop.com.

posts.body:
OpenAI just announced it is "Advancing computer use with Ironclad."

Computer use means the AI can click through a screen for you, not just answer in a chat box. It fills forms, moves between tabs, finishes a task end to end.

Everyone will write about what Ironclad does. Here is what it means for a freelancer running ads with no team behind them.

Right now, most "automation" in a small ad account is you, at 11pm, copying a lead from a Meta notification into a spreadsheet. Computer use tools are built to do exactly that step — the boring click between two screens that nobody automated because it was too small to bother with.

That is also the exact gap that loses money today. Across nine Meta ad accounts I've run, nothing captured what happened after a lead came in. No reorder timing, no follow-up, a "not interested" treated as final — and some of those leads came back on their own, months later, and ordered.

A tool that can click through screens doesn't fix a strategy problem. It fixes a nobody-got-around-to-it problem. Those are most of what actually breaks in a small business.

Open your own lead form today. Where does a submission land — your inbox, a sheet, nowhere? What's the last manual step between a lead coming in and someone actually calling them?

posts.hook: OpenAI just announced ads inside ChatGPT: "Building advertising for the way people use AI." Everyone will post the headline this week. The part worth your Monday is what it changes for a small ad account.
posts.body:
OpenAI just announced ads inside ChatGPT: "Building advertising for the way people use AI."

Everyone will post the headline this week. The part worth your Monday is what it changes for a small ad account.

ChatGPT ads will show up where people ask questions, not scroll. That's a different kind of attention than Meta or Google ever sold you.

On Meta, you win the first glance. On ChatGPT, you may only get picked when someone is already asking for an answer.

That changes what "the ad" even is. It's less a banner competing for eyes, more an answer competing to be the one recommended.

If you run a small business, nothing to set up today. There's no self-serve dashboard live yet for someone your size.

What you can do now: write down, in plain words, what question a stranger would type right before they'd want your product.

That sentence is what you'll be bidding to answer, whenever this opens up. Start collecting them.

Everything else — budgets, targeting, creative — will still matter. It just moves a layer upstream, to the question, not the headline.

posts.body:
Google Ads & Commerce just pushed a fresh round of updates to how products show up in Shopping and across Google's surfaces.

Most small business owners never check the one setting this actually touches: the product feed. The feed is the file that tells Google what you sell, the price, the stock status. Not the ad. The ad just points at the feed.

Here's the part nobody checks. Open Merchant Center, go to Diagnostics, and look for disapproved or warning items. If your feed has errors, no amount of fixing the ad creative or the budget changes what Google shows. The feed is the product. The ad is just the poster for it.

This matters more now because Google keeps folding more of Shopping into AI-driven surfaces — the kind that pull straight from feed data, not from the ad copy you wrote. A clean feed used to be a nice-to-have. It is becoming the only lever that works.

Cost per lead, click-through rate, creative testing — all downstream of whether Google can even read your catalogue correctly.

Open Merchant Center today. Go to Diagnostics. How many items are sitting in "disapproved" right now, and do you know why?

posts.body:
Meta just named Dhruv Vohra to lead its Southeast Asia business.

A leadership change at Meta doesn't touch your ad account directly. But it's a reminder that the platform your budget runs on is run by people making decisions you never see — and the only defence is knowing exactly what you can check yourself, today, without waiting on anyone.

Most people running their own ads have never opened the one screen that shows what Meta is actually optimising for. It's not in the creative. It's not in the budget. It's one line, three clicks in, called the Performance goal.

If that line says "maximise number of leads" when you meant "maximise quality," Meta will hand you volume and call it a win. Nobody at Meta checks this for you. Nobody at any agency checks it unless they're told to.

This isn't about the reshuffle. It's about not waiting for a headline to go check your own account.

slides.text: Meta just changed who runs its Southeast Asia business.
That news means nothing to your ad account. One setting near it does.
Every Meta ad campaign has a line called the Performance goal, hidden inside the ad set.
It tells Meta what to chase — leads, clicks, calls, or something else entirely.
Most people never open it. They judge the campaign from the creative instead.
Set it to 'maximise number of leads' and Meta will hand you volume, not fit.
Set it to 'maximise conversion value' and it starts chasing something closer to a sale.
Nobody at Meta flags this for you. Not before you spend, not after.
Here's where it lives: Ads Manager → your campaign → the ad set → Performance goal.
